lesson.title: Not Enough Electrons to Go Around: Incomplete Octets
lesson.summary: A handful of stable molecules, especially those built around beryllium or boron, are perfectly happy with fewer than eight electrons surrounding the central atom, a pattern called an incomplete octet.
lesson.body:
The octet rule predicts that atoms want 8 electrons around them, but a small set of elements, most notably beryllium and boron, routinely form stable neutral molecules where the central atom has fewer than 8. This happens because these elements simply do not have enough valence electrons to reach an octet even after forming as many bonds as their geometry allows, and unlike period 3 and higher elements, they have no low energy way to draw additional bonds, such as double bonds, that would fill the gap without violating other rules.

Boron trifluoride, BF3, is the standard example. Total valence electrons: boron contributes 3, and three fluorines contribute 7 each, 21, for 3 plus 21 equals 24. Boron forms three B-F single bonds, using 6 electrons, leaving 18 electrons, which become 3 lone pairs, 6 electrons, on each fluorine. Boron itself ends up with only 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs, meaning just 6 electrons surround it, two short of a full octet.

You might wonder why fluorine does not just form a double bond to boron to fill that gap. It could, formally, but doing so would place a positive formal charge on the highly electronegative fluorine and a negative formal charge on boron, which is chemically backwards, since electronegative atoms should carry negative, not positive, formal charge. Because that alternative structure is less reasonable by formal charge standards, chemists accept the incomplete octet on boron as the more realistic depiction, and the actual bonding and reactivity of BF3 confirm it.

That electron deficiency is not a flaw, it is the whole reason BF3 is chemically useful. With only 6 electrons around it, boron has an empty orbital and readily accepts a lone pair from another molecule, acting as what is called a Lewis acid. Beryllium compounds show the same pattern for a similar reason: beryllium has only 2 valence electrons, so beryllium chloride, BeCl2, in its simple gas phase form, forms just two Be-Cl bonds and ends up with only 4 electrons around beryllium, a lone pair short of even boron's total. Carbocations, positively charged carbon species that show up throughout organic chemistry, are another example: the methyl cation, CH3+, has a carbon that forms three C-H bonds, using 6 electrons, with no lone pair, leaving carbon with only 6 electrons around it, just like boron in BF3.

Incomplete octets are the mirror image of expanded octets, both are genuine exceptions to the octet rule, just in opposite directions: one has too few electrons, the other too many. Recognizing an incomplete octet takes the same electron counting process you already use for every Lewis structure: total the valence electrons, place the bonds, distribute lone pairs to outer atoms, and if the central atom cannot reach 8 electrons even after every atom has a reasonable structure, accept the incomplete octet rather than forcing an unrealistic double bond.
